learn.title: A function that calls itself
learn.body: Recursion means a function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of the same problem. You met this shape in merge sort: sort the halves, then combine. Now we study it directly.

learn.title: A countdown
learn.body: `countdown(3)` prints 3, then calls `countdown(2)`, and so on. When `n` reaches 0 it prints liftoff and stops.

learn.title: Following countdown(3)
learn.body: Each call waits while the next one runs.
steps: `countdown(0)` prints liftoff and returns. The others then return too

learn.title: Two parts
learn.body: Every recursive function has an easy case that it answers directly, and a step that moves toward it by calling itself with a smaller input. Here the easy case is `n == 0` and each call uses `n - 1`.
Trust the call. When writing a recursive function, assume the call on the smaller input already works, and only write the step that uses it.

choices: A function calling itself on a smaller problem
questions.explanation: The function solves a bigger problem using the same function on a smaller one.
It prints 2, calls `countdown(1)` which prints 1, then `countdown(0)` prints liftoff.

questions.prompt: How many numbers (not counting liftoff) does `countdown(3)` print?
In `countdown`, each recursive call uses the argument \_\_.
questions.explanation: Each call gets a smaller number, so the calls approach the stopping point.

questions.prompt: Put the lines printed by `countdown(2)` in order.
questions.explanation: The number is printed before the recursive call, so the larger number comes first.
That branch returns without calling `countdown` again.

questions.prompt: When does each call of `countdown` finish?
choices: After the call it made has returned
Only at the end of the program
questions.explanation: A call waits for the call it started to return, then returns itself.
